Platelet coagulation prevention

Some red or near-infrared protocols reduced platelet aggregation or reactivity, while a green-light experiment increased aggregation under selected conditions. A pig bypass model reported less platelet destruction. No patient trial has shown fewer clots or bleeding events.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Some red or near-infrared protocols reduced platelet aggregation or reactivity, while a green-light experiment increased aggregation under selected conditions. A pig bypass model reported less platelet destruction. No patient trial has shown fewer clots or bleeding events.

Summary of the Evidence

Ten publications are mapped to platelet or platelet-related coagulation outcomes: nine are in the platelet category and one concerns platelet loss during cardiopulmonary bypass in pigs. Eight reports use in-vitro or ex-vivo methods, and two include animal work. One 2025 publication combines mouse experiments with observational human data; the human data are not a clinical PBM intervention. Method counts overlap within publications, and these studies measure mechanisms or blood-product quality rather than patient outcomes.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical trial has treated patients with PBM to prevent thrombosis or bleeding. One publication includes observational human information alongside experiments in mice, but it does not show that exposing patients to PBM changes their clinical risk. A separate ex-vivo study used human blood to test red light and nitrite in coagulation assays; those samples were studied outside the body and do not establish treatment efficacy (Wajih et al. 2021).

Animal evidence

In mice, visible red-light exposure was associated with reduced platelet aggregation and changes in thrombus-related outcomes. In a pig cardiopulmonary-bypass model, light treatment reduced platelet destruction during extracorporeal circulation. Both are experimental models, not evidence that the approach prevents thrombosis or bleeding in patients (Andraska et al. 2025).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The laboratory reports do not point in one uniform direction. Near-infrared exposure of porcine blood reversibly reduced platelet reactivity and modestly reduced hemolysis, with effects depending on dose. Other experiments found anti-aggregatory effects with red light, while a green-light experiment increased aggregation in the presence of weak agonists. A platelet-storage study using near-infrared light reported changes in activation markers and metabolism but did not show that stored platelets improved patient outcomes (Walski et al. 2022).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The database spans blue visible light near 442 or 488 nm, green visible light near 532 nm, red or far-red visible light near 617–662 nm, and near-infrared exposures from about 700 to 1000 nm. Some blood was irradiated outside the body; other work used animal exposure or platelet storage bags. Reported doses are inconsistent or absent, and results cannot be treated as one standard PBM protocol. No patient trial or clinical dose-finding comparison was identified.

Interpretation

Some red- and near-infrared-light experiments reported reduced platelet aggregation or reactivity, and a pig cardiopulmonary-bypass model found less platelet destruction. A green-light experiment increased aggregation in the presence of weak agonists. Thus, platelet responses were not uniformly anti-clotting and depended on wavelength and experimental conditions. No clinical study shows that PBM prevents thrombosis or improves bleeding outcomes.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for preventing thrombosis or bleeding outcomes in patients Very low, mechanistic evidence for platelet changes under specific exposures
Publications and records10 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Laboratory and animal studies report both reduced platelet aggregation or reactivity and increased aggregation under selected wavelengths or conditions; a pig bypass model also found less platelet destruction. The direction depends on exposure and model. No patient trial has shown fewer clots or bleeding events. Standardized independent studies and controlled clinical outcomes would be needed to support a stronger clinical claim.
